summary: Formally specifies the Robots Exclusion Protocol, the robots.txt method originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994 for site owners to control how automatic crawlers may access their content. It adds formal definition language, error handling rules, and caching instructions. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A sign on a website's door tells search robots which rooms they may enter. This writes the sign language down as an official standard.

questions: what is the robots exclusion protocol
how long can crawlers cache robots.txt
subtitle: The rules a website uses in robots.txt to tell automated crawlers which parts of the site they may visit.

tldr.problem: Service owners may not want crawlers to visit their whole URI space, and the original 1994 robots.txt convention left details such as syntax, error handling and caching loosely defined.
tldr.mechanism: A plain-text file named /robots.txt holds groups of user-agent lines followed by allow and disallow rules. Crawlers pick the group that matches their product token and apply the most specific matching rule.
tldr.outcome: The convention is now a Proposed Standard with a formal grammar, rules for fetch failures and redirects, a 24-hour caching guideline and a minimum parsing limit. The rules are a request to crawlers, not access control.

facts.label: Cache limit
facts.value: No more than 24 hours (SHOULD NOT exceed)

today: RFC 9309 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2022, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It documents the 1994 convention that its text describes as originally defined by Martijn Koster.

sections.title: What the Robots Exclusion Protocol Is
sections.content:
RFC 9309 specifies the Robots Exclusion Protocol, a method originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994. It lets service owners say how automatic clients called crawlers may access the content they serve. Search engines are the example the RFC gives: their crawlers recursively traverse links to index content.

The document adds a formal definition language, instructions for handling errors and instructions for caching. It applies to services whose resources are reached through URIs as defined in RFC 3986.

The RFC states plainly that these rules are not a form of access authorization. Crawlers are requested to honor them.
sections.eli5: A website can put up a note saying which pages robots should leave alone. The note is a request, like a 'please do not touch' sign, not a locked door.

sections.title: Rules and Groups
sections.content:
The protocol language consists of rules and groups, made available in a file named robots.txt. A rule is a line with a key-value pair that defines how a crawler may access URIs. A group is one or more user-agent lines followed by one or more rules. A group ends at the next user-agent line or at the end of the file.

The last group may have no rules, which means it implicitly allows everything. The formal grammar is written in ABNF (RFC 5234). Lines may carry trailing comments introduced by a hash sign, empty lines are allowed, and keys such as user-agent, allow and disallow are written in lowercase in the grammar.
sections.eli5: The file is a list of mini-notes. Each mini-note starts by naming which robots it is for, then lists the places those robots may or may not go.

sections.title: Choosing a Group and Matching Paths
sections.content:
Each crawler has a name called a product token. It MUST contain only letters, underscores and hyphens, and SHOULD be a substring of the identification string the crawler sends, such as the HTTP User-Agent header. Crawlers MUST match the product token case-insensitively. If several groups match, their rules MUST be combined into one group. If none matches, the crawler MUST obey the group whose user-agent value is a lone asterisk, if present. If there is none, no rules apply.

To decide whether a URI is allowed, the crawler matches the paths of allow and disallow rules against it. Matching SHOULD be case sensitive and MUST start with the first octet of the path. The most specific match, meaning the one with the most octets, MUST be used. If an allow and a disallow rule are equivalent, the allow rule SHOULD be used. If nothing matches, the URI is allowed, and /robots.txt itself is implicitly allowed.

Octets outside ASCII and those in the reserved range of RFC 3986 MUST be percent-encoded before comparison. A percent-encoded ASCII octet in the URI MUST be unencoded first, unless it is a reserved character or outside the unreserved range.
sections.eli5: A robot finds the note with its own name on it, or the note for 'all robots' if there is none. If two rules both fit a page, the one that spells out more of the address wins.

sections.title: Special Characters and Other Records
sections.content:
Crawlers MUST support three special characters in rules: the hash sign starts a comment, the dollar sign marks the end of the match pattern, and the asterisk matches zero or more instances of any character. To match one of these characters literally in a URI, crawlers SHOULD use percent-encoding, so /path/foo-%24 matches a URI ending in foo-$.

Crawlers MAY interpret other records that are not part of the protocol, with Sitemaps as the example. They MAY be lenient, for instance by accepting common misspellings. Parsing such records MUST NOT interfere with the defined ones, so a Sitemaps record MUST NOT terminate a group.
sections.eli5: Two symbols work like wildcards in a game: a star means 'anything can go here' and a dollar sign means 'the address stops right here'.

sections.title: Fetching robots.txt and Handling Failures
sections.content:
The rules MUST be available in a file named /robots.txt, all lowercase, in the top-level path of the service. The file MUST be UTF-8 encoded and have Internet Media Type text/plain. For HTTP the example is https://www.example.com/robots.txt; the RFC also shows an FTP example.

What the crawler does depends on the outcome of the fetch:

  • Success: the crawler MUST follow the parseable rules.
  • Redirects: crawlers SHOULD follow at least five consecutive redirects, even across authorities. If the file is reached within five, it is used in the context of the initial authority. After more than five, crawlers MAY assume the file is unavailable.
  • Unavailable (HTTP status codes in the 400-499 range): the crawler MAY access any resources on the server.
  • Unreachable (server or network errors, HTTP 500-599): the file is undefined and the crawler MUST assume complete disallow. If this lasts a reasonably long period, for example 30 days, crawlers MAY treat the file as unavailable or keep using a cached copy.
  • Parsing errors: crawlers MUST try to parse each line and MUST use the parseable rules.
sections.eli5: If the sign is missing, robots may walk in. If the website is broken and the robot cannot read the sign, it must stay out to be safe.

sections.title: Caching and Parsing Limits
sections.content:
Crawlers MAY cache the fetched file and MAY use standard cache control as defined in RFC 9111. They SHOULD NOT use the cached version for more than 24 hours, unless the file is unreachable.

To protect their systems, crawlers SHOULD impose a parsing limit. That limit MUST be at least 500 kibibytes, so a site owner can rely on at least the first 500 KiB of the file being processed.
sections.eli5: A robot may remember the sign for a day, but then it should look again. It must also be willing to read at least a very long list, though it can stop at some point.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol is not a substitute for real content security. Listing paths in robots.txt exposes them publicly and makes them discoverable. To actually control access, site owners should use a valid security measure for the application layer, such as HTTP Authentication from RFC 9110.

Implementors of parsers should treat the file as untrusted content, reject out-of-bound characters as invalid, and rely on the minimum parsing limit of Section 2.5 to guard against out-of-memory scenarios. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Writing 'secret room, keep out' on a public sign tells everyone where the secret room is. If something really must stay private, it needs a lock.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's simple example has four groups. The group for all user agents disallows every path ending in .gif and /example/, but allows /publications/. The foobot group disallows / and then allows only /example/page.html and /example/allowed.gif. A shared group for barbot and bazbot disallows /example/page.html. The final quxbot group is empty, so that crawler has unrestricted access.

The longest-match example shows Allow: /example/page/ next to Disallow: /example/page/disallowed.gif. The longer rule wins for that file.
sections.eli5: Different robots get different notes: one is shut out of nearly everything, another can go anywhere, and when two rules clash the more detailed one wins.

data.title: robots.txt
data.code:
User-Agent: *
Disallow: *.gif$
Disallow: /example/
Allow: /publications/

User-Agent: foobot
Disallow:/
Allow:/example/page.html
Allow:/example/allowed.gif

User-Agent: barbot
User-Agent: bazbot
Disallow: /example/page.html

User-Agent: quxbot

EOF

items.label: End anchor
items.desc: Designates the end of the match pattern.

items.label: Wildcard
items.desc: Designates 0 or more instances of any character.
